f.p: Confederación Indígena Tayrona
f.t: The Confederación Indígena Tayrona, the Arhuaco organization founded in 1976, plans to restore the Guatapurí river basin with 18,000 native trees.

f.p: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage
f.t: In 2022 UNESCO inscribed the ancestral knowledge system of the Arhuaco, Kankuamo, Kogui and Wiwa peoples as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

f.p: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones
f.t: For the Arhuaco, weaving mochilas, ruanas and clothing is also a way of passing on thought, tradition and their understanding of the world.

n.l: South-eastern slopes of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta in Cesar and Magdalena, northern Colombia

f.p: Instituto Nacional de Estadística de Bolivia
f.t: In Bolivia's 2024 census, more than one million people self-identified as Aymara, and more than one million as Quechua.

f.p: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios
f.t: Aymara is a vital language in Peru, where the 2017 census counted 450,010 people who learned to speak it in childhood.

n.l: The altiplano around Lake Titicaca and nearby valleys and cities of Bolivia and Peru, and the far north of Chile

f.p: Instituto Nacional de Estadísticas de Chile
f.t: In Chile's 2024 census, 0.1 percent of the national population identified as Colla.

f.p: Museo Chileno de Arte Precolombino
f.t: The first Colla Indigenous communities in Chile were officially constituted in the early 1990s.

f.p: Museo Chileno de Arte Precolombino
f.t: Colla communities in Chile are found in Atacama Region areas such as Potrerillos and Inca de Oro, in Chañaral, Copiapó and Tierra Amarilla.

n.l: Atacama Region of Chile, around Copiapó, Chañaral, Tierra Amarilla and Diego de Almagro, and the puna of northwestern Argentina

f.p: Museo Chileno de Arte Precolombino
f.t: The first Diaguita community constituted under Chile's Indigenous Law, the Estancia Agrícola Diaguita de los Huascoaltinos, formed in 2006.

f.p: Museo Chileno de Arte Precolombino
f.t: Many people who self-identify as Diaguita in Chile live in the upper Huasco River basin, in the municipality of Alto del Carmen.

n.l: Huasco and Choapa valleys of Chile's Norte Chico, and northwestern Argentina

f.p: Organización Gonawindúa Tayrona
f.t: The Organización Gonawindúa Tayrona serves as the representative body of the Kággaba people's own Indigenous government.

n.l: Northern, eastern and western slopes of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta in La Guajira, Magdalena and Cesar, Colombia

f.p: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage
f.t: In 2022 UNESCO recognized the ancestral knowledge system shared by the Kankuamo, Arhuaco, Kogui and Wiwa as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

f.p: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones
f.t: The Kankuamo resguardo, about 24,212 hectares near Valledupar, was collectively titled to the people in 2003.

f.p: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones
f.t: Since the late 1980s, supported by neighboring Sierra Nevada peoples, the Kankuamo have led a process of cultural renewal and peaceful resistance.

n.l: South-eastern foothills of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta near Valledupar, Cesar, Colombia, centered on Atánquez

f.p: Ministerio de Salud Pública del Ecuador
f.t: In Cañar parish, the province's largest Indigenous organizational network brings together 15 communities and 5 cooperatives.

f.p: Ministerio de Salud Pública del Ecuador
f.t: The Kañari keep a vigorous ethnic identity and a very strong organizational system, in which cooperatives and many kinds of organizations are very active.

f.p: Ministerio de Salud Pública del Ecuador
f.t: Kañari communities trade foods and seeds between higher and lower altitude zones, and their lively exchange networks also reach other regions, especially Ecuador's coast.

n.l: Cañar and Azuay provinces in the southern highlands of Ecuador

f.p: Asamblea Nacional del Ecuador
f.t: The Confederación del Pueblo Kayambi holds a General Assembly where its communities and organizations bring their proposals and demands.

f.p: Asamblea Nacional del Ecuador
f.t: In 2022 Kayambi water boards, communes and community organizations met with a national legislator to discuss issues including a new water law.

n.l: Around Cayambe in Pichincha province and neighboring areas of Imbabura, northern Ecuador

f.p: Cultural Survival
f.t: Hampiriypacha, a Kichwa Otavalo association of seed guardians, works to protect knowledge that women have passed down for generations.

f.p: Cultural Survival
f.t: Yarina, a Kichwa Otavalo family band started in 1984, plays original Indigenous rhythms on traditional Andean instruments and works to keep Kichwa traditions alive.

n.l: Otavalo and nearby communities such as Peguche in Imbabura province, northern Ecuador

f.p: Ministerio de Salud Pública del Ecuador
f.t: Ecuador's 2010 census counted 136,141 Kichwa Puruwá people, about 18.5 percent of the whole Kichwa nationality.

f.p: Ministerio de Salud Pública del Ecuador
f.t: The Puruwá people include the communities of Cacha, Colta, Licto and Guamote in Chimborazo, each with its own local character.

n.l: Chimborazo province in the central highlands of Ecuador

f.p: Cultural Survival
f.t: In 2019 Radio Kipa, a new community radio station in Saraguro, was one of the few radios to have won a license from Ecuador's state in recent years, and planned to train 30 young people.

f.p: Cultural Survival
f.t: CORPUKIS, a coordinating body of Kichwa Saraguro organizations, works with grassroots groups to advance civil, human and collective rights in its territory.

n.l: Saraguro canton in Loja province and nearby areas of southern Ecuador

f.p: Asamblea Nacional del Ecuador
f.t: Ecuador's Constitution names Kichwa, together with Spanish and Shuar, as official languages of intercultural relations.

f.p: Asamblea Nacional del Ecuador
f.t: In 2009 Ecuador's Constitution was translated into Kichwa, with five delegates from Indigenous communities reviewing the translation.

n.l: Highland provinces of Ecuador along the Andes, from Imbabura and Pichincha south to Chimborazo, Cañar and Loja

f.p: Ministerio de las Culturas, las Artes y el Patrimonio de Chile
f.t: Lickanantay communities are revitalizing their language, Ckunsa. A 2025 regional arts project in Chiu Chiu promotes it through art and stop-motion animation.

f.p: Instituto Nacional de Estadísticas de Chile
f.t: In Chile's 2024 census, 0.2 percent of the national population identified as Atacameño or Lickanantay.

f.p: Museo Chileno de Arte Precolombino
f.t: Lickanantay communities live in the oases and valleys of the Atacama salt flat and the Loa river basin in Chile's Antofagasta Region.

n.l: Oases and valleys of the Salar de Atacama and the Loa river basin, Antofagasta Region, northern Chile

f.p: Museo Chileno de Arte Precolombino
f.t: Most Mapuche in Chile today live in cities, with the largest groups in La Araucanía region and in the capital, Santiago.

f.p: Museo Chileno de Arte Precolombino
f.t: Mapudungun, the Mapuche language, is still the most widely spoken Indigenous language in Chile.

n.l: South-central Chile, especially La Araucanía and Santiago, and Patagonian provinces of Argentina such as Neuquén and Río Negro

f.p: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones
f.t: Misak traditional dress, including the man's blue wrap called lusi pal, stands as a lasting symbol of resistance and of how the Misak present themselves.

n.l: Resguardos of Guambía and Quisgó in Silvia, Cauca, and nearby municipalities of southwestern Colombia

f.p: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones
f.t: The Nasa language is Nasa Yuwe. In Colombia's 2005 census, 41.9 percent of Nasa people reported speaking it.

n.l: Cauca department, especially Tierradentro and northern Cauca, with communities in Huila, Valle del Cauca, Tolima and Putumayo, Colombia

f.p: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones
f.t: The Pasto are working to recover their identity, oral tradition and ancestral customs, and to strengthen their own law through their cabildos.

f.p: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones
f.t: Most Pasto communities live in resguardos dating from colonial times and in other lands in Nariño, such as Cumbal, Guachucal, Ipiales and Túquerres.

n.l: Highlands of Nariño, Colombia, in municipalities such as Cumbal, Guachucal, Ipiales and Túquerres, and across the border in northern Ecuador

f.p: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios
f.t: Peru's Ministry of Culture reports that 5,179,774 people nationwide feel or consider themselves part of the Quechua peoples.

f.p: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios
f.t: Peru's Ministry of Culture lists Quechua as a vital language, and the 2017 census counted 3,805,531 people who learned to speak it in childhood.

f.p: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage
f.t: Each year four Quechua-speaking communities in Peru's southern Andes rebuild the Q'eswachaka rope bridge over the Apurímac River with Inca techniques. UNESCO recognized it in 2013.

n.l: Andean highlands and valleys of Peru and Bolivia, with Quechua communities also in Argentina and Chile

f.p: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios
f.t: In Peru's 2017 census, 681 people self-identified as part of the Uro people.

f.p: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios
f.t: For centuries the Uro have lived on large rafts of totora reed, called floating islands, on Lake Titicaca in the Bay of Puno, and many Uro families still live on them.

f.p: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios
f.t: Uro communities today are working to recover knowledge of their ancestral language, with support from Peru's Ministry of Culture.

n.l: Lake Titicaca, especially the Bay of Puno in Peru, with Uru communities also in Bolivia

f.p: Órgano Electoral Plurinacional de Bolivia, Fuente Directa
f.t: The Uru Chipaya statute recognizes the Uru Chipaya language as an official language of their autonomous government.

f.p: Órgano Electoral Plurinacional de Bolivia, Fuente Directa
f.t: The Uru Chipaya nation approved its own autonomy statute by referendum in 2016 and in 2017 became one of Bolivia's first three Indigenous self-governments.

f.p: Órgano Electoral Plurinacional de Bolivia, Fuente Directa
f.t: Leadership of the Uru Chipaya executive rotates in turns among the nation's four ayllus: Aranzaya, Manazaya, Wistrullani and Ayparavi.

n.l: Chipaya, on the altiplano of Oruro department, Bolivia

f.p: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones
f.t: Through education policies the Wiwa established an alphabet for Damana, and they are working to have it taught alongside Spanish in schools.

f.p: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones
f.t: Wiwa mochilas include the duadu, woven from pure cotton for personal belongings, and the suzu, made of fique fiber with colorful designs.

n.l: Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta in La Guajira, Cesar and Magdalena, Colombia

f.p: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones
f.t: Yanacona leader Juan Gregorio Palechor, of the Guachicono resguardo, was among the community leaders who formed the CRIC in Cauca in 1971.

f.p: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones
f.t: The Yanacona are recovering their identity and culture, including their traditional language, Quechua, and strengthening their cabildo authorities.

f.p: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones
f.t: Yanacona territory covers a large part of the Macizo Colombiano, the mountain region of southern Cauca.

n.l: The Macizo Colombiano in southern Cauca, with communities in Huila and Valle del Cauca, Colombia
